Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- China's giant pandas are believed to be safe after Monday's earthquake, but concern is growing over how they will get their next meals. The giant pandas' primary food source is bamboo. Authorities confirmed Tuesday that captive animals in two of China's major panda reserves were alive, according to Xinhua, China's official news agency. The Wolong Giant Panda Reserve Center in southwest Sichuan province is home to about 86 giant pandas, who were reported safe Tuesday. Staff and critters at neighboring Chengdu Panda Breeding and Research Center were also reported safe, according to a spokesperson for the Atlanta Zoo, which has two pandas on loan from the wildlife reserve. Concern arose in the international wildlife community over damage to the animals' habitat, as authorities continued assessing the scope of damage in the Sichuan province. The mountainous, densely wooded region is the natural habitat for most of the 1,200 giant pandas living in the wild, making it an obvious location for research bases like Wolong and Chengdu. Giant pandas roam the forest in "open cages" that are meant to provide them with a safe, natural environment that will prepare them for release. With the safety of the pandas confirmed, the animals' caregivers are left to determine how resources like food and medical supplies will reach the bases, which contain breeding facilities and triage centers. Bamboo, the pandas' primary source of food, is a major agricultural product in the region, but whether it can be supplied to the pandas despite infrastructure damage is open to question. "Wolong is hard to access under normal conditions, so the heavy road damage makes it even harder," said Kerry Zobor, spokesperson for the World Wildlife Fund. Zobor said WWF had confirmed the safety of staff based in Beijing, but had not received word on the conditions in Wolong. She said the WWF was also concerned about members who had been touring the country when the earthquake struck. So far, the group has not been located. Scientists in the United States are hopeful that Chinese researchers will adapt to the situation facing them. David Wildt with the Smithsonian's National Zoological Park in Washington says that scientists in Wolong have overcome threats to the giant panda population before. In the late 1990s, the captive giant panda population was in decline, with more animals dying than were born, Wildt said. Thanks to a collaborative effort with American scientists, the Wolong staff was able to reverse the trend. "Our Chinese colleagues are very perceptive when it comes to addressing problems," said Wildt, who has visited Wolong many times as part of the Smithsonian's affiliation with the research base. "Because of their efforts, the population is on the rise today." Wildt said that Chinese scientists have also addressed the issue of alternative food sources before. "Artificial diets in the form of protein biscuits have been created for giant pandas. They're not a complete substitute, but they meet the needs of a basic high-fiber diet," said Wildt, who has worked with two pandas that the Smithsonian has on loan from Wolong. "Right now, we're mostly concerned about the staff. If the staff is fine, then the animals will be fine," Wildt said.

(CNN) -- Following Monday’s earthquake, China’s giant pandas are thought to have survived unharmed, though worries are increasing about how food will be delivered to them. Bamboo is the main part of a giant panda’s diet.

On Tuesday, Chinese officials said that pandas kept at two of the country’s major panda reserves were alive, according to Xinhua, China’s state-run news agency. At the Wolong Giant Panda Reserve Center in southwestern Sichuan province, roughly 86 pandas were reported to be safe. Employees and animals at the nearby Chengdu Panda Breeding and Research Center were also said to be unharmed, according to a representative of Zoo Atlanta, which has two pandas on loan from that reserve.

As officials continued to evaluate the destruction across Sichuan province, wildlife experts around the world became increasingly concerned about harm to panda habitat. The region, which is mountainous and heavily forested, is the natural home of most of the estimated 1,200 giant pandas that live in the wild. That makes it a natural setting for research centers such as Wolong and Chengdu.

The pandas live in forested “open cages,” areas designed to give them a protected but natural setting that can help prepare them for eventual release. Now that the pandas’ survival has been confirmed, caretakers must figure out how to get necessities such as food and medical supplies to the research bases, which include breeding facilities and emergency care centers.

Although bamboo is widely grown in the area and is the pandas’ chief food, it remains uncertain whether it can be delivered to them because of damage to roads and other infrastructure.

“Wolong is hard to access under normal conditions, so the heavy road damage makes it even harder,” said Kerry Zobor, a spokesperson for the World Wildlife Fund.

Zobor said WWF had confirmed that its Beijing-based staff members were safe, but the organization had not yet received information about conditions in Wolong. She added that WWF was also worried about members who had been traveling in China when the quake hit. As of that time, they had not been found.

Researchers in the United States expressed hope that their Chinese counterparts would be able to adjust to the emergency. David Wildt of the Smithsonian’s National Zoological Park in Washington said scientists at Wolong had previously dealt successfully with serious risks to the giant panda population.

Wildt said that in the late 1990s, the captive panda population was shrinking, with deaths outnumbering births. Through cooperation with American scientists, Wolong staff managed to turn that pattern around.

“Our Chinese colleagues are very perceptive when it comes to addressing problems,” said Wildt, who has traveled to Wolong many times through the Smithsonian’s partnership with the research center. “Because of their efforts, the population is on the rise today.”

Wildt also noted that Chinese researchers have previously worked on backup food options for pandas.

“Artificial diets in the form of protein biscuits have been created for giant pandas. They’re not a complete substitute, but they meet the needs of a basic high-fiber diet,” said Wildt, who has worked with two pandas on loan to the Smithsonian from Wolong.

“At the moment, our greatest concern is for the staff,” Wildt said. “If the staff is all right, the animals should be all right too.”

**Panda reserves assess damage, bamboo supplies after Sichuan earthquake**

**CHENGDU, China** — Wildlife officials in southwestern China were working to assess the condition of giant pandas and their food supplies after the powerful Sichuan earthquake damaged roads, cut communications and raised concerns about access to major panda facilities.

The Wolong National Nature Reserve, one of China’s best-known panda breeding and research centers, was among the facilities affected by the quake. The reserve lies in mountainous terrain near the epicenter, where landslides and collapsed roads made it difficult for rescuers and supplies to reach the site.

Initial reports indicated that many of the pandas at Wolong survived, but the extent of damage to enclosures, research buildings and surrounding habitat remained a concern. Officials and staff were also working to determine whether enough bamboo — the animals’ primary food source — could be delivered or gathered safely.

Giant pandas eat large quantities of bamboo each day, and any disruption to supply routes can quickly become a problem for captive animals. Landslides triggered by the earthquake also threatened bamboo forests in the region, raising longer-term worries about habitat conditions.

At the Chengdu Research Base of Giant Panda Breeding, farther from the worst-hit mountain areas, the situation appeared more stable. The facility reported less severe damage and continued caring for its pandas, though officials were monitoring transportation routes and supply chains as aftershocks continued.

Access remained one of the biggest challenges. Roads into Wolong were reportedly blocked or damaged, slowing efforts to bring in food, medical supplies and repair crews. Communication outages complicated efforts to confirm the status of staff, animals and infrastructure.

China’s giant panda centers play a central role in the country’s conservation program for the endangered species. The earthquake added an urgent logistical challenge: keeping pandas fed and secure while rescuers focused on broader disaster response across Sichuan province.

counterfactuals.output:
**BREAKING NEWS: China quake damages panda reserves in Sichuan; conservationists scramble to assess losses**

**CHENGDU, China —** Monday’s powerful earthquake in southwestern China has struck at the heart of giant panda country, damaging roads, cutting communications and raising urgent concerns about panda reserves across Sichuan province, home to most of the world’s remaining wild pandas.

The quake, centered near Wenchuan County, was felt across a region that includes several key panda habitats and breeding facilities, including the famed Wolong National Nature Reserve, one of China’s most important centers for panda conservation.

Early reports from conservation groups indicated that the full extent of damage remained unclear because landslides and collapsed roads had isolated mountain reserves. The immediate priority, officials and conservationists said, was confirming the safety of staff and animals and restoring access to affected facilities.

Kerry Zobor, a spokesperson for the World Wildlife Fund, said WWF was working to gather information from partners in the region.

> “Sichuan is the core of giant panda habitat, so any major earthquake there is deeply concerning,” Zobor said. “Right now, the challenge is simply getting reliable information from reserves that may be cut off by damaged roads and communications.”

Wolong, located in steep mountain terrain, is considered especially vulnerable to earthquake-triggered landslides. The reserve has long served as a flagship site for panda breeding, research and reintroduction work. Conservationists said damage to enclosures, veterinary facilities and bamboo forests could pose risks even if pandas survived the initial shaking.

David Wildt, a senior scientist at the Smithsonian’s National Zoo who has worked on giant panda reproduction and conservation, said the disaster could have both immediate and long-term effects.

> “The first concern is the safety of the people and the animals,” Wildt said. “But for pandas, habitat is everything. Landslides can destroy bamboo stands, fragment forest corridors and make it harder for wild pandas to move and feed.”

China’s giant panda reserves are spread through mountainous areas of Sichuan, Shaanxi and Gansu provinces, but Sichuan contains the largest share of protected panda habitat. The region’s rugged landscape has helped shelter pandas from development, yet the same terrain makes rescue and damage assessment difficult after earthquakes.

Conservationists warned that even limited damage could be significant for a species that remains vulnerable despite decades of recovery efforts. Wild pandas rely almost entirely on bamboo, and disruptions to bamboo forests or access routes could complicate both animal care and field monitoring.

Zobor said WWF expected the conservation response to unfold in stages.

> “Once emergency crews can reach these areas, there will need to be a careful assessment of damage to panda facilities and surrounding habitat,” she said. “This is not just about buildings. It’s about the forest ecosystem that pandas depend on.”

Chinese authorities have not yet released a complete assessment of the quake’s impact on panda populations. Rescue teams and reserve staff were believed to be checking breeding centers, patrol stations and remote habitat areas as conditions allowed.

Wildt said the resilience of panda conservation programs would be tested in the coming days.

> “China has invested enormously in panda conservation,” he said. “That work gives these animals a better chance, but a disaster of this scale can still set back local efforts, especially if habitat and infrastructure are badly damaged.”

Officials and conservation groups said more information was expected as roads reopen and communication with remote reserves is restored.

counterfactuals.output:
# Pandas Face Safety, Habitat, and Feeding Challenges After Sichuan Earthquake

Reports from Xinhua, Zoo Atlanta, WWF, and the Smithsonian’s National Zoo described serious concerns for giant pandas after the devastating Sichuan earthquake, focusing on the safety of pandas and staff, damage to habitat and facilities, and the difficulty of maintaining reliable food supplies.

The earthquake struck Sichuan Province, one of the most important regions for wild and captive giant pandas. Xinhua reported that panda reserves and breeding centers were affected, with landslides, damaged roads, and communication failures complicating rescue and assessment efforts. The Wolong National Nature Reserve, a major panda conservation and breeding site near the quake zone, was among the areas of greatest concern. Buildings were damaged, access routes were blocked, and staff worked under dangerous conditions to protect the animals.

Zoo Atlanta, which has long participated in giant panda conservation and breeding programs, emphasized the immediate safety of pandas and caregivers. Its updates noted concern for animals at Chinese panda facilities and for the keepers and researchers responsible for them. While captive pandas were generally reported to have survived, the situation remained difficult because damaged enclosures, aftershocks, and disrupted infrastructure created continuing risks.

WWF focused heavily on the earthquake’s impact on panda habitat. The organization warned that the quake and resulting landslides may have damaged large areas of forest in the Minshan and Qionglai mountain ranges, key strongholds for wild giant pandas. Habitat fragmentation was already a major threat before the disaster, and WWF noted that landslides, collapsed slopes, and damaged roads could further isolate panda populations or reduce access to bamboo. The group also stressed that recovery should consider both human needs and the long-term protection of panda habitat.

The Smithsonian’s National Zoo highlighted another urgent concern: feeding. Giant pandas depend almost entirely on bamboo, and captive pandas require a steady daily supply. After the earthquake, blocked roads and damaged transport networks made it harder to deliver bamboo to affected centers. The Smithsonian noted that any interruption in food supply could quickly become serious because pandas eat large quantities of bamboo every day. Conservation staff therefore had to ensure that pandas had enough food while also repairing enclosures and monitoring animal health.

Together, the reports showed that the earthquake posed both immediate and long-term challenges. In the short term, rescuers and keepers had to secure pandas, repair damaged facilities, restore communication, and maintain bamboo supplies. In the long term, conservationists faced the harder task of assessing damage to wild panda habitat and ensuring that reconstruction did not further threaten fragile ecosystems.

Although many pandas survived the disaster, the Sichuan earthquake underscored how vulnerable the species remains. Giant panda conservation depends not only on breeding centers and reserves, but also on stable mountain forests, reliable bamboo growth, and safe access for the people who care for them.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.output:
**CNN NEWS SEGMENT SCRIPT**  
**Title:** *After the Quake: Sichuan’s Giant Pandas Face a Fragile Recovery*  
**Length:** ~3–4 minutes  

---

**[OPENING SHOT]**  
*Wide aerial images of Sichuan’s mountainous terrain. Broken roads, landslide scars, mist over forested valleys. Cut to archival or current footage of giant pandas in enclosures and bamboo forests.*

**ANCHOR:**  
In China’s Sichuan Province, the aftermath of a powerful earthquake has left communities rebuilding — and raised urgent concerns for one of the region’s most iconic residents: the giant panda.  

From the remote panda habitats around **Wolong** to the conservation facilities in **Chengdu**, caretakers and wildlife experts are working to protect both captive and wild pandas after landslides, damaged roads, and disrupted bamboo supplies threatened their survival.

---

**[CUT TO: CORRESPONDENT ON LOCATION IN SICHUAN]**  
*Reporter standing near a mountainous road with visible landslide damage or repair crews in the background.*

**CORRESPONDENT:**  
Here in Sichuan, the earthquake’s impact goes far beyond collapsed buildings and blocked roads. This region is the heart of China’s panda country — home to some of the world’s most important giant panda conservation sites.  

One of the hardest-hit areas is **Wolong**, long known as a key panda reserve and research base. The rugged terrain that makes it an ideal habitat for pandas also makes rescue and recovery efforts extremely difficult. Landslides have damaged access routes, making it harder to deliver food, medical supplies, and equipment.

---

**[B-ROLL]**  
*Pandas eating bamboo. Workers carrying bamboo bundles. Veterinarians examining pandas. Damaged mountain roads.*

**CORRESPONDENT:**  
For pandas in captivity, the immediate concern is food. Giant pandas eat bamboo almost exclusively, consuming large amounts every day. But after the quake, bamboo supplies became harder to transport. Roads were blocked, forests were disrupted, and some local bamboo sources were damaged or temporarily inaccessible.

Conservation staff have been racing to bring in fresh bamboo from safer areas. At facilities like the **Chengdu Panda Breeding and Research Center**, teams have been coordinating bamboo deliveries, checking animals for stress, and preparing backup feeding plans if supplies run short.

---

**[CUT TO: INTERVIEW — PANDA CARETAKER / CONSERVATION EXPERT]**

**CARETAKER:**  
Pandas are very sensitive to changes in their environment. After an earthquake, they may become frightened, stop eating normally, or show signs of stress. Our first priority is to make sure they are safe, calm, and have enough bamboo.

---

**[B-ROLL]**  
*Panda cubs in nursery areas. Staff cleaning enclosures. Emergency supplies stacked outside a conservation center.*

**CORRESPONDENT:**  
The **Chengdu Panda Breeding and Research Center** has become an important support hub, not only for pandas already in its care, but also for wider conservation efforts across the region. Staff there monitor panda health, manage breeding programs, and can help receive or temporarily shelter animals if conditions at other sites become unsafe.

But bamboo remains the biggest challenge. Pandas are famously picky eaters, and they do not consume every type of bamboo. They prefer certain species and parts of the plant depending on the season — leaves, stems, or shoots. That makes emergency feeding more complicated than simply finding any bamboo.

---

**[GRAPHIC ON SCREEN]**  
**PANDA DIET IN AN EMERGENCY**  
- Fresh bamboo: primary food source  
- Bamboo shoots, leaves, stems: seasonally preferred  
- Supplemental foods: apples, carrots, specially prepared “panda bread”  
- Veterinary monitoring required  

---

**ANCHOR VOICEOVER:**  
When bamboo is limited, caretakers may use **alternative panda diets** as short-term supplements. These can include apples, carrots, steamed corn bread, and specially formulated high-fiber cakes sometimes called “panda bread.”  

But experts stress these foods are not replacements for bamboo. They are emergency supplements, used carefully to maintain energy and hydration while fresh bamboo supplies are restored.

---

**[CUT BACK TO CORRESPONDENT]**

**CORRESPONDENT:**  
For wild pandas, the situation is even more difficult to assess. Many live in dense, mountainous forests where landslides may have destroyed bamboo stands or fragmented habitat. Scientists worry that damaged corridors could make it harder for pandas to move between feeding areas, find mates, or avoid human activity as rebuilding expands.

Teams are expected to use field surveys, camera traps, and signs such as droppings and feeding traces to determine whether wild pandas have been displaced or cut off from food sources.

---

**[B-ROLL]**  
*Forest rangers walking through bamboo. Camera traps being installed. A panda moving through forest footage.*

**WILDLIFE EXPERT:**  
The danger for wild pandas is not only the earthquake itself. It’s what comes after — landslides, habitat fragmentation, reduced bamboo access, and human disturbance during reconstruction. Protecting corridors is essential.

---

**[CUT TO: MAP GRAPHIC]**  
*Map of Sichuan showing Chengdu, Wolong, and surrounding panda habitat areas.*

**CORRESPONDENT:**  
Wolong remains central to this recovery. The reserve has historically played a major role in panda protection, research, and breeding. Any damage there affects not just individual animals, but decades of conservation work.

At the same time, Chengdu’s panda facilities are helping demonstrate how emergency planning can reduce risk — with stored supplies, veterinary teams, backup transport routes, and coordinated bamboo sourcing.

---

**[CUT TO: PANDA ENCLOSURE]**  
*A panda sits calmly eating bamboo. Staff observe from a distance.*

**CORRESPONDENT:**  
There are encouraging signs. Many pandas in managed care have been accounted for, and caretakers say animals that were initially frightened are beginning to return to normal feeding and resting patterns. Still, recovery will take time.

The priority now: keep bamboo moving, keep veterinary teams deployed, and make sure rebuilding does not further damage the fragile mountain forests wild pandas depend on.
